rv.q: His performance is staggering in its physical discipline, its piercing emotional transparency and, most surprisingly, its restraint.
He shines as Merrick, never overplaying his grotesqueness.
And we say good for him and his smashing, heart-ripping portrayal.

This is a beautifully judged Broadway revival, from the sleek design and swift pace to the professionalism of the supporting cast — in particular, Henry Stram as Carr Gomm and Anthony Heald as the bishop.
The ever-fine Clarkson is a marvel of sympathetic restraint.
Mr. Cooper brings a mixture of childlike wonder and adult anguish to John Merrick that makes you forget you're watching a movie star slumming on Broadway.
If the effect is slightly hollow, the performance, and the production, are at least broadly satisfying.
But the play that surrounds him has come to seem somewhat brittle and artificial.
However, strong acting cannot soften wooden dialogue or smooth bumpy transitions.
It's no slight to Cooper, in fact, to say that this gorgeous Elephant Man is a shared achievement.
What's really on view are man's inhumanity and a topnotch Cooper.
That said, each of these actors very much belongs on a Broadway stage.
This “Elephant Man” will be best remembered for its deeply committed performance by Cooper, who joins a long line of actors—Hurt, Philip Anglim, David Bowie, Bruce Davison—to play him.
Much of the play is tediously consumed by Treves debating notions of morality and normalcy with his colleagues. But even if the play lacks narrative power, the setup is still fascinating.
"The Elephant Man" can be ponderous but there's nothing like a thrilling performance to lift a heavy show well off the ground.
Cooperemploying a lilting, singsongy gentleman's English to suggest the gentle Merrickowns this production.
Cooper can’t be blamed, however, for playing Merrick the way Pomerance wrote him: The guy is a saintly bore.

A mix of cruelty and humanity, a bit of voyeurism, and some fascination at an indomitable human spirit are the stuff of Bernard Pomerance‘s play “The Elephant Man,” in a moving revival directed by Scott Ellis.

cn.t: Cooper delivers a transformative, physically committed performance that anchors this solid but somewhat creaky revival of Pomerance's 1977 drama, though the production itself proves more workmanlike than revelatory.
